case_study_insert.main_stem: Meridian Rail Freight (MRF) is a private limited company in the rail freight industry, operating container and bulk trains between the coast port and inland terminals across the country. Founded in 2009 by Idris Bakare, it employs a workforce of 120 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. MRF plans to invest $1,150,000 in two new electric locomotives and an upgraded inland freight terminal on the port-Midlands corridor, financed by a $650,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $34 a unit and a selling price of $58, and currently produces 30,000 units a year. MRF faces one operational problem: absenteeism among train drivers has reached 8% and is disrupting schedule reliability.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2026: MRF's intermodal services achieved 91.2% on-time performance in Q3 2026, up from 84.6% a year earlier. Average turnaround at the port terminal was 5.4 hours, down from 6.8 hours. Customer complaints fell from 24 to 15 per month. Market research of 480 freight buyers found that 58% would switch providers for guaranteed sub-6-hour terminal turnaround and 61% require rail carbon reporting in supplier selection. A driver training needs analysis shows 18 of 120 drivers have not completed simulator refresher training; courses at the national rail academy cost $750 per driver. A training needs analysis found that 18 drivers need on-the-job training on the new locomotive diagrams and off-the-job training at the national rail academy before the full service launch.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Rail Freight for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, the third rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $13.10 to $13.87 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills in transport and warehousing. (3) Commercial electricity and wholesale diesel costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while rail freight volumes grew 2.8% as retailers shifted goods from road to rail.

questions.question_text: MRF plans to fund part of its electric locomotive investment with a $650,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for MRF of using retained profit to fund the expansion rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs MRF nothing in interest, which protects the business at a time when commercial electricity has risen 14.2% and its fixed costs already stand at $420,000 a year. Every dollar not paid to the bank can be retained to absorb the input-cost inflation in traction energy, helping MRF hold its $58 selling price and its 91.2% on-time performance standard while the port-Midlands corridor ramps up.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the risk attached to borrowing at a time when the base interest rate has risen from 5.25% to 6.0% and may rise again. If MRF funds the $1,150,000 expansion from its own reserves, Idris Bakare and the existing shareholders keep full control of when the two electric locomotives enter service, with no lender covenant restricting how the inland terminal upgrade is phased. It also preserves borrowing headroom for future wagon purchases that self-funding would consume.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Meridian Rail Freight and its locomotive expansion decision.

questions.question_text: MRF is launching its new electric locomotive container service on the port-Midlands corridor. Consider a trade press advertising campaign in logistics magazines, sponsorship of the national rail industry conference, or a dedicated contracts team approaching freight forwarders directly. Which should MRF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade press advertising: Advertising in logistics magazines would reach freight buyers and fleet managers with detailed copy about the electric locomotives' emissions credentials and the 5.4-hour terminal turnaround. It is credible among industry readers and relatively affordable, but readership is broad and largely uncontracted; many readers work for rival carriers or road hauliers, so wastage of spend is high for a single-corridor launch backed by a $1,150,000 commitment, and it generates enquiries, not signed volume.

Sponsorship of the national rail industry conference: Sponsorship would position MRF strongly with the exact firms that specify rail contracts, generate face-to-face leads, and reinforce its attendance at a time when 61% of surveyed buyers require rail carbon reporting. However, conference sponsorship is expensive for one or two days a year, coverage ends when the event closes, and competitors exhibit alongside MRF, diluting exclusivity.

Dedicated contracts team: A small contracts team calling on freight forwarders directly converts the 58% of 480 surveyed buyers ready to switch providers for guaranteed sub-6-hour turnaround into written agreements, tailoring capacity commitments to each forwarder's volumes. It is slower to scale than advertising and carries salary costs, but it targets the highest-intent buyers and matches the B2B nature of rail freight.

Recommendation: MRF should choose the dedicated contracts team. Rail freight is bought through negotiated contracts, not spot purchases, so direct selling captures the switching-intent segment that advertising can only reach passively; the conference is rejected as too brief and shared with rivals, and trade press alone is rejected as too untargeted and non-binding to secure corridor volumes. MRF can use the 91.2% on-time rate and 5.4-hour turnaround as the team's proof points, adding modest conference presence only as supporting credibility.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotion options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MRF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MRF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade press and conference sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: MRF's train driver absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for MRF of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its rail operations team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives MRF's 120 employees, especially the train drivers affected by the 8% absenteeism, a real voice in how rosters, simulator refresher schedules and terminal shift patterns are set. Being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, so drivers ordered into new locomotive diagrams feel ownership of the timetable, directly lowering absenteeism and the resulting 6.8-to-5.4-hour turnaround gains slippage that MRF has worked to achieve.

Point 2: Involving operations staff in decisions surfaces practical improvements from the people running the corridor daily — for example smarter braking patterns, depot handover routines or maintenance windows that protect the 91.2% on-time rate. Higher involvement lifts morale and reduces labour turnover among scarce qualified drivers, saving the $750 per driver refresher training cost at the national rail academy and protecting output of 30,000 units while the $1,150,000 terminal upgrade disrupts normal operations. Consultation through shift representatives and the existing hierarchical chain of command also gives Idris Bakare early warning of rostering grievances before they flare into further absence, protecting the 5.4-hour turnaround already achieved.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MRF's absenteeism, on-time performance and output.

questions.question_text: MRF must train 18 drivers on the new electric locomotives. Consider on-the-job training on the railway line or off-the-job training at the national rail academy. Which should MRF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training aboard MRF's own electric locomotives on the port-Midlands corridor is directly relevant to the exact traction, braking and fault routines drivers will face, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 18 drivers productive while learning, protecting the 91.2% on-time performance during the locomotive introduction. Drawbacks are that experienced corridor drivers act as trainers at the expense of their own diagrams, bad habits transfer unchecked, and no externally recognised certification is issued, which matters if the port authority or insurers demand formal licences for electric-worked freight.

Off-the-job training: The national rail academy course at $750 per driver gives all 18 structured, simulator-based electric-traction instruction and a recognised certificate, costing $13,500 in total — small against the $1,150,000 investment. It removes 18 of 120 drivers from rostered duties at once, however, potentially denting terminal turnaround towards the old 6.8-hour level, and generic academy content may not match MRF's specific route and terminal working, so on-site consolidation would still be needed.

Decision: MRF should choose on-the-job training supported by the academy simulator for the two lead drivers, rather than full off-the-job cover. It is cheaper, keeps the corridor running at 5.4 hours, and builds fleet-specific competence immediately; the academy's recognised certificates can be added later once the service stabilises. Blanket off-the-job training is rejected because pulling 18 drivers off the roster during the launch would directly reverse the turnaround gains and on-time performance that MRF is selling to freight buyers, and because the $13,500 academy bill, however small against the expansion, buys less route-specific competence than targeted line training when the fleet is brand new and every failure is a learning signal worth capturing at the point of work.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of MRF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of MRF with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and route relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MRF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($58 − $34) = $420,000 ÷ $24 = 17,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 17,500 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $58 − $34 = $24.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $24.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MRF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. MRF's managers can compare the 17,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 30,000 units to confirm the electrified corridor is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 12,500 units, informing whether to add a second electric service pattern.
2. Contribution per unit of $24 lets MRF model discounts negotiated with freight forwarders, for example a price cut to $55 would drop contribution to $21, letting managers judge whether extra switch-over volume still covers the $420,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $420,000 and contribution per unit helps managers stress-test repayments on the $650,000 bank loan and the $1,150,000 expansion before committing to further terminal capacity, protecting cash while electricity costs rise 14.2%.
4. Managers can use average total cost of $48.00 ($420,000 ÷ 30,000 + $34) to benchmark traction efficiency across quarters, target the schedule disruption behind the 8% driver absenteeism, and benchmark against road hauliers when defending the $58 selling price.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 17,500 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $24.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 12,500 units vs 30,000-unit output; forwarder discount modelling vs $420,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $650,000 bank loan and $1,150,000 expansion; and average total cost benchmarking at $48.00 to tackle absenteeism-related schedule disruption.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MRF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MRF's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue = $3,600,000 and gross profit = $1,440,000 against cost of sales of $2,160,000; 2025 revenue = $4,200,000 and gross profit = $1,890,000 against cost of sales of $2,310,000. 2024 operating profit = $360,000 against $3,600,000 of revenue (10.0%); 2025 operating profit = $630,000 against $4,200,000 of revenue (15.0%). 2024 capital employed = $2,400,000, 2025 = $3,000,000; interest payable rose from $84,000 to $112,000 after the larger borrowing for the locomotive programme. 2024 figure: $360,000 ÷ $2,400,000 = 15.0% on capital employed; 2025 figure: $630,000 ÷ $3,000,000 = 21.0%.

Evaluation: MRF's profitability has clearly strengthened. Margins widened on both measures because revenue grew $600,000 while cost of sales grew only $150,000, evidence of better load factors on the electrified corridor and the fuel saving the two electric locomotives will extend. The operating profit figure rose by $270,000, outpacing the moderate rise in interest payable, so borrowing is comfortably serviced while the 2.8% growth in rail volumes favours contracted freight. However, capital employed grew 25% from $2,400,000 to $3,000,000, so future returns must keep pace with that larger base; interest at 6.0% will sting if the $650,000 loan re-prices, and contracted freight forwarders paying late could strain working capital even though margins are strong.

Conclusion: MRF's financial performance has improved. Gross profit margin rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, the operating profit margin rose from 10.0% to 15.0%, and ROCE rose from 15.0% to 21.0%, all exactly the trend MRF needs ahead of its $1,150,000 expansion. The improvement is broad-based, not one-off, but depends on protecting cost control and timely customer payments as the new locomotives bed in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether MRF's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MRF of introducing electric locomotives on the port-Midlands corridor.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Electric locomotives cut traction emissions, which speaks directly to the 61% of the 480 surveyed freight buyers who require rail carbon reporting in supplier selection and the 58% ready to switch providers for guaranteed sub-6-hour terminal turnaround. MRF could win multi-year contracted volume on the port-Midlands corridor, protect its $58 selling price against road carriers facing diesel volatility, and strengthen its case when negotiating priority slots with the port authority.

Disadvantage: The $1,150,000 investment is concentrated capital that must earn back before road hauliers undercut on price, and commercial electricity has risen 14.2% year-on-year, eating into the fuel-saving case exactly when fixed costs stand at $420,000. Any unreliability of the charging and terminal power supply would also undermine the 91.2% on-time performance MRF promotes, and a locomotive breakdown would hit the single port-Midlands corridor harder than a diversified diesel fleet. Battery and traction-equipment replacement economics must also be checked against the ten-year bank loan, because rail regulators and insurers will ask hard questions of a new technology on a live freight path.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MRF's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in commercial electricity and diesel costs will affect MRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If MRF's $650,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 0.75%, adding about $4,875 a year to financing costs and slightly raising the cash burden beyond its $420,000 fixed costs. Higher rates also make freight buyers more cautious with capital projects and could raise the cost of topping up the locomotive finance, though MRF can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate before April. The direct effect is real but modest, and dwarfed by operating costs.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.87 per hour): With 120 staff — drivers, terminal crew and office — MRF's wage bill will rise by roughly 5.9%. If average hourly pay is around $13.87, one full-time employee costs roughly $28,900 a year, so a 5.9% rise adds about $1,700 per worker, or roughly $204,000 across the workforce. That is a larger cash hit than the interest increase and lands hardest on terminal turnaround shifts and driver rosters during the launch. Democratic leadership and the simulator refresher programme can offset it through productivity, but wages are unavoidable.

Input cost inflation (14.2% electricity and diesel): MRF's $34 variable cost per unit is dominated by traction energy. A 14.2% rise on an energy component of even half the $34 — say $17 — adds about $2.41 per unit, or roughly $72,300 a year at 30,000 units, and cuts contribution per unit from $24.00 toward $21.60. Because energy feeds every single train, not just payroll, the drag is structural and hits the margin that justifies the $1,150,000 investment.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in commercial electricity and diesel costs will have the greatest impact. It erodes the $24 contribution on every one of the 30,000 units sold, compounding to roughly $70,000 a year and threatening the recovery of the electrification investment itself at the very moment rail volumes grow only 2.8%. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious pressure and will need careful rostering and productivity gains, while the interest rate increase is the smallest in cash terms and manageable by fixing the loan rate; both still demand tighter cost control and firmer contract pricing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MRF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MRF with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
